routes.label: Compare circle areas under the equal-size assumption

question:
Six pepperoni circles will exactly fit across the diameter of a \(12\)-inch pizza when placed as shown. If a total of \(24\) circles of pepperoni are placed on this pizza without overlap, what fraction of the pizza is covered by pepperoni?

[Figure 1](figures/2010_AMC_8_Q10_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
Assume that all \(24\) pepperoni circles are equal in size. Then the six circles spanning the pizza's diameter divide its \(12\)-inch length into six equal diameters.

[Figure 1](figures/2010_AMC_8_Q10_question_fig1.svg)

Each pepperoni circle therefore has diameter \(12\div6=2\) inches and radius \(1\) inch. The pizza has radius \(12\div2=6\) inches. Using the circle-area formula \(A=\pi r^2\), one pepperoni circle has area \(\pi\) square inches, and the pizza has area \(36\pi\) square inches.

Because the pepperoni circles do not overlap, their areas add. Thus the covered fraction is
\[
\frac{24\pi}{36\pi}=\boxed{\frac23},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\) under the equal-size assumption.

Without that assumption, the written conditions do not determine a unique fraction. Start with any allowed placement of \(24\) circles, keep the six pictured circles unchanged, and shrink one of the other \(18\) circles about its center. It remains on the pizza without overlapping any other circle, but its area decreases. The covered fraction therefore changes while the stated conditions remain satisfied.
